questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Basis of assets — purchased property, gift basis (carryover/FMV limit for loss), inherited property (§1014 step-up), converted property, wash sale rule §1091, organization/start-up costs §195/§248
questions.text: A taxpayer inherits stock from a deceased relative who paid $10,000 for the stock. At the date of death, the stock's fair market value is $85,000. The taxpayer sells the stock for $90,000 nine months after inheriting it. What is the taxpayer's basis in the stock and the character of the gain?

answers.text: Basis = $85,000 (FMV at date of death — §1014 stepped-up basis); gain = $5,000 long-term capital gain (inherited property is always long-term)
Basis = $10,000 (carryover basis from decedent); gain = $80,000 short-term capital gain (held 9 months)
Basis = $47,500 (average of purchase price and FMV at death); gain = $42,500 long-term capital gain
Basis = $85,000; gain = $5,000 short-term capital gain (held only 9 months after inheritance)

explanations.a: Section §1014 — inherited property basis: (1) Basis = FMV at date of death = $85,000 (regardless of the decedent's original $10,000 cost — the basis is 'stepped up' to FMV); (2) Gain on sale = $90,000 − $85,000 = $5,000; (3) Character: ALL inherited property, regardless of how long the heir actually holds it, is classified as LONG-TERM capital gain when sold. The holding period rule for inherited property: the property is deemed to have been held for MORE THAN ONE YEAR, even if the heir holds it for only one day. This special long-term treatment means the taxpayer pays the preferential LTCG rate (0/15/20%) on the $5,000 gain, not the short-term ordinary rate. The step-up in basis eliminates the $75,000 of built-in gain the decedent never paid tax on — a significant estate planning benefit.
explanations.b: Inherited property does NOT take the decedent's carryover basis. Under §1014, the heir's basis is the FAIR MARKET VALUE at the date of death (stepped-up basis) — this eliminates the built-in gain that accumulated during the decedent's lifetime.
explanations.c: There is no averaging formula for inherited property basis. §1014 mandates FMV at date of death as the heir's basis — not an average of purchase price and FMV.
explanations.d: The 9-month actual holding period does not determine the character. §1014 grants ALL inherited property automatic long-term status — this is a specific statutory override of the normal 12-month holding period requirement.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Basis of assets — purchased property, gift basis (carryover/FMV limit for loss), inherited property (§1014 step-up), converted property, wash sale rule §1091, organization/start-up costs §195/§248
questions.text: Maria received stock as a gift when the stock's FMV was $15,000. The donor's adjusted basis was $22,000 and the donor paid no gift tax. Maria later sells the stock. Calculate Maria's basis for GAIN purposes and for LOSS purposes.

answers.text: Gain basis: $22,000; Loss basis: $22,000 — the donor's carryover basis always applies to gifts
Gain basis: $22,000 (donor's carryover basis); Loss basis: $15,000 (FMV at gift date) — the dual-basis rule applies because FMV at gift was less than the donor's basis
Gain basis: $15,000 (FMV at gift date); Loss basis: $15,000 — FMV at gift date always determines the donee's basis
Gain basis: $22,000; Loss basis: $22,000 — gift basis always equals the donor's original purchase price

explanations.a: When FMV at gift date is LESS than the donor's adjusted basis, the standard carryover basis rule is modified. The donee's basis is NOT simply the donor's basis for both gain and loss — the dual-basis rule applies.
explanations.b: Gift basis rules under §1015 — the DUAL BASIS rule: When FMV at gift date < Donor's adjusted basis (a 'loss' gift): (1) For purposes of computing GAIN: the donee's basis = DONOR'S ADJUSTED BASIS ($22,000). If Maria sells for MORE than $22,000, she computes gain on $22,000 basis. (2) For purposes of computing LOSS: the donee's basis = FMV AT DATE OF GIFT ($15,000). If Maria sells for LESS than $15,000, she computes loss on $15,000 basis. (3) No gain or loss zone: if Maria sells for between $15,000 and $22,000 (e.g., $18,000), she neither recognizes gain (sale price $18,000 < gain basis $22,000) nor loss (sale price $18,000 > loss basis $15,000). This creates a 'built-in loss preservation' rule — it prevents the donee from recognizing a loss that existed when the property was transferred as a gift.
explanations.c: If FMV at gift is LESS than the donor's basis, the donee's basis for GAIN is the donor's higher basis (to prevent the gain from disappearing), not FMV. Using FMV for gain would allow the loss embedded in the gift to disappear entirely.
explanations.d: Gift basis is the donor's ADJUSTED basis (not original purchase price — they could be different if the donor took depreciation or made improvements). Additionally, for loss purposes when FMV < donor's basis, the loss basis is FMV, not the donor's adjusted basis.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Basis of assets — purchased property, gift basis (carryover/FMV limit for loss), inherited property (§1014 step-up), converted property, wash sale rule §1091, organization/start-up costs §195/§248
questions.text: On March 1, a taxpayer sells 100 shares of XYZ stock for $8,000, realizing a $3,000 loss (basis = $11,000). On March 20, the taxpayer purchases 100 shares of XYZ stock for $9,000. Apply the wash sale rule and determine the tax consequences.

answers.text: The $3,000 loss is fully deductible in the current year — the wash sale rule only applies if the replacement shares are purchased BEFORE the original shares are sold
The $3,000 loss is disallowed and permanently lost — the wash sale rule eliminates the loss with no basis adjustment to the replacement shares

The $3,000 loss is disallowed under §1091 because substantially identical shares were purchased within 30 days after the sale; the disallowed $3,000 loss is added to the basis of the replacement shares, making their adjusted basis $12,000
The wash sale rule applies only to losses on stocks held for less than one year; since no holding period is specified, the loss is deductible

explanations.a: The wash sale rule under §1091 applies to purchases within 30 days BEFORE OR AFTER the sale. The March 20 purchase is 19 days after the March 1 sale — within the 30-day window. The loss is disallowed regardless of which transaction occurs first.
explanations.b: The wash sale rule defers the loss (adds it to basis of replacement shares) — it does not permanently eliminate it. The $3,000 is preserved in the basis of the new shares.
explanations.c: Wash sale rule (§1091): A loss from the sale of stock or securities is DISALLOWED if the taxpayer acquires substantially identical securities within the 61-day wash sale period (30 days before to 30 days after the sale date). Analysis: March 1 sale creates $3,000 loss. March 20 purchase (19 days after sale) = within 30-day post-sale window → WASH SALE. The $3,000 loss is DISALLOWED for the current year. However, the disallowed loss is NOT permanently lost — it is ADDED TO THE BASIS of the replacement shares: New basis of replacement shares = $9,000 (purchase price) + $3,000 (disallowed loss) = $12,000. The holding period of the replacement shares also includes the holding period of the sold shares. Effect: when the replacement shares are later sold, the increased $12,000 basis will reduce the recognized gain (or increase the recognized loss) — the $3,000 loss deduction is deferred, not eliminated.
explanations.d: The wash sale rule applies to ANY loss on sales of stock or securities, regardless of holding period. Short-term and long-term losses are equally subject to §1091.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Basis of assets — purchased property, gift basis (carryover/FMV limit for loss), inherited property (§1014 step-up), converted property, wash sale rule §1091, organization/start-up costs §195/§248
questions.text: Two entrepreneurs start a corporation on January 1. Before the business opens, they incur: legal fees for incorporation $4,000; state filing fees $800; market research for the business plan $12,000; salaries paid to train employees before opening $8,000; advertising prior to opening $5,000. Total pre-opening costs: $29,800. Classify and determine the tax treatment of each cost.

answers.text: All $29,800 of pre-opening costs must be capitalized and have no deduction until the corporation is sold or liquidated
All $29,800 are immediately deductible in the year they are incurred as ordinary and necessary business expenses under §162
Organization costs ($4,800) are permanent capital expenditures with no deduction; start-up costs ($25,000) are immediately expensed under §195

Organization costs (§248): $4,800; Start-up costs (§195): $25,000; Each category gets $5,000 immediate deduction (reduced if costs exceed $50,000) with the remainder amortized over 180 months beginning with the month the active trade or business begins

explanations.a: Pre-opening costs are not simply held in limbo until sale/liquidation. IRC specifically provides deduction mechanisms for both organization costs (§248) and start-up costs (§195) — deferring ALL costs until disposition would significantly over-burden new businesses.
explanations.b: Pre-opening costs are NOT immediately deductible under §162 because the business is not yet active. Section 162 requires an ACTIVE trade or business — costs incurred before business commences do not qualify for immediate deduction (hence the need for §195 and §248).
explanations.c: Organization costs ARE deductible (under §248 election), not permanently capitalized. Start-up costs under §195 are NOT fully immediately expensed — only $5,000 is immediately deductible; the rest is amortized over 180 months.
explanations.d: Classification and treatment: ORGANIZATION COSTS (§248) — costs of creating the corporation itself: Legal fees for incorporation: $4,000; State filing fees: $800. Total organization costs: $4,800. TREATMENT: elect to deduct up to $5,000 immediately (reduced dollar-for-dollar by organization costs exceeding $50,000); remainder amortized over 180 months. Since $4,800 < $5,000, the full $4,800 is immediately deductible. START-UP COSTS (§195) — costs incurred before the active trade or business begins that would be deductible if incurred after opening: Market research: $12,000; Employee training: $8,000; Pre-opening advertising: $5,000. Total start-up costs: $25,000. TREATMENT: elect to deduct up to $5,000 immediately (reduced dollar-for-dollar when total costs exceed $50,000); remainder amortized over 180 months. Since $25,000 < $50,000, the full $5,000 can be deducted immediately; $20,000 is amortized over 180 months (≈$111/month). Total year 1 deductions: $4,800 (org costs) + $5,000 immediate + partial month's amortization (≈$67 if opened Jan 1).

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Cost recovery — MACRS depreciation (recovery periods, half-year/mid-quarter convention, §168(k) bonus depreciation, §179 expensing); §197 amortization; listed property limitations
questions.text: A calendar-year taxpayer places a $50,000 piece of 5-year MACRS property into service on July 1. Assuming the half-year convention applies and the MACRS first-year rate for 5-year property is 20%, what is the first-year depreciation deduction?

answers.text: $10,000 — the full 20% applies to the $50,000 cost because the asset was placed in service on July 1
$5,000 — under the half-year convention, only 50% of the annual depreciation is allowed in the first year regardless of the actual placement date
$4,167 — depreciation is calculated from the actual date of service (July 1 = 6 months remaining) at 20% × 6/12
$10,000 — 20% × $50,000 = $10,000; the half-year convention is applied in the SECOND year, not the first

explanations.a: Under the MACRS half-year convention, ALL personal property placed in service at ANY point during the tax year is treated as if it were placed in service at the midpoint of the year (July 1 for a calendar-year taxpayer). This means the PUBLISHED MACRS RATE already incorporates the half-year convention — the first-year rate of 20% is already the HALF-YEAR-ADJUSTED rate. Applying it to the full cost: 20% × $50,000 = $10,000. The taxpayer does NOT further reduce this by another 50% — doing so would double-apply the convention. The MACRS percentage tables for 5-year property (20%, 32%, 19.2%, 11.52%, 11.52%, 5.76% for years 1-6) already reflect the half-year convention built into each year's rate.
explanations.b: This answer incorrectly applies another 50% reduction (50% × $10,000 = $5,000) to the already-convention-adjusted MACRS rate. The 20% first-year MACRS rate IS the half-year-convention-adjusted rate — applying 50% again would produce the wrong result.
explanations.c: MACRS does not pro-rate based on actual months in service. The half-year convention treats ALL personal property as placed in service on July 1, regardless of the actual date — this simplification is built into the published rates.
explanations.d: The half-year convention is reflected in ALL years' MACRS percentages. Year 2's rate (32%) also reflects the half-year convention. There is no 'second-year adjustment' because all rates already incorporate the convention.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Cost recovery — MACRS depreciation (recovery periods, half-year/mid-quarter convention, §168(k) bonus depreciation, §179 expensing); §197 amortization; listed property limitations
questions.text: A business purchases $1,800,000 of 7-year MACRS equipment in January. The §179 expensing limit is $1,220,000 (with phase-out starting at $3,050,000). Bonus depreciation under §168(k) is 60% for the current year. The business has $900,000 of taxable income before any depreciation. Calculate the maximum first-year cost recovery deduction.

answers.text: §179 deduction: $1,220,000 (no phase-out since $1,800,000 < $3,050,000); remaining basis: $580,000; bonus depreciation: 60% × $580,000 = $348,000; regular MACRS on remaining: ($580,000 − $348,000) × 14.29% = $33,153; total first-year: $1,601,153 — but limited to not create NOL? §179 is limited to taxable income but bonus and regular MACRS can create a loss
§179 deduction: $900,000 (limited to business taxable income before depreciation); remaining basis: $900,000; bonus: 60% × $900,000 = $540,000; total limited by taxable income
Total deduction = $1,080,000 (60% × $1,800,000 bonus only) — §179 is not combined with bonus depreciation

explanations.a: Same calculation as C — both reach the same total of approximately $1,601,153. Option C adds the clarification about the §179 taxable income limitation.
explanations.b: Full calculation using §179 up to $1,220,000 (no phase-out) then bonus on remainder: §179 = $1,220,000; remaining basis = $580,000; bonus = 60% × $580,000 = $348,000; regular MACRS on $232,000 remaining × 14.29% = $33,153; total = $1,601,153. §179 income limitation: §179 cannot exceed business taxable income before §179 ($900,000). So §179 is capped at $900,000. But bonus depreciation has no income limitation and can create/increase an NOL. This makes the total deduction complex to compute without more information about applying the $900,000 §179 cap. The key insight: §179 limited by income; bonus depreciation not limited by income.
explanations.c: §179 is limited to TAXABLE INCOME from active conduct of trade or business ($900,000 before depreciation). However, §179 is applied FIRST and can be taken up to the income limit — unused §179 carryforward to next year. But then bonus depreciation is applied to the remaining basis (not the §179-reduced basis here). Let me re-analyze: §179 is limited to $900,000 by the income limitation; remaining after §179: $1,800,000 − $900,000 = $900,000; bonus depreciation: 60% × $900,000 = $540,000; regular MACRS: ($900,000 − $540,000) × 14.29% = $51,444; total = $900,000 + $540,000 + $51,444 = $1,491,444. Income limitation: §179 up to $900,000 taxable income — after §179 of $900,000, taxable income = $0. Bonus and MACRS can then create an NOL. Option B correctly identifies the income limitation issue.
explanations.d: §179 and bonus depreciation CAN be combined — they work in sequence: §179 first reduces basis, then bonus depreciation applies to the remaining basis, then regular MACRS on the remaining balance.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Cost recovery — MACRS depreciation (recovery periods, half-year/mid-quarter convention, §168(k) bonus depreciation, §179 expensing); §197 amortization; listed property limitations
questions.text: A company acquires another business and pays $2,000,000 for the following identifiable intangible assets: customer list $400,000; trade name $300,000; covenant not to compete (5-year term) $200,000; goodwill $1,100,000. How should these intangibles be amortized for tax purposes?

answers.text: Goodwill and trade name: not amortizable (indefinite life); customer list: amortized over 5 years; covenant: amortized over its 5-year contractual term
Goodwill is not deductible; other intangibles are amortized over their useful lives as determined by accounting standards
All four intangibles are §197 intangibles and are amortized ratably over 15 years (180 months) on a straight-line basis, beginning with the month of acquisition
All intangibles are immediately expensed under §195 as start-up costs in the year of acquisition

explanations.a: This describes the GAAP (financial accounting) treatment for intangibles, not the tax treatment. Under GAAP, goodwill and indefinite-lived intangibles are not amortized (tested for impairment). For TAX purposes under §197, acquired intangibles (including goodwill, trade names, customer lists, and covenants) are ALL amortized over 15 years, regardless of their economic or legal lives.
explanations.b: Under §197, goodwill IS amortizable for tax purposes — this is a major difference from GAAP treatment. The $1,100,000 of goodwill generates $73,333/year of tax amortization over 15 years.
explanations.c: IRC §197 — amortization of acquired intangible assets: For intangibles ACQUIRED as part of a trade or business (or the acquisition of assets constituting a trade or business), §197 requires 15-year straight-line amortization beginning with the month of acquisition. §197 intangibles include: goodwill, going-concern value, workforce in place, business books and records/systems, patents, copyrights (if acquired as part of a business), customer lists, trade names, franchises, licenses, and covenants not to compete. Annual amortization: $2,000,000 / 180 months × 12 = $133,333/year. Key feature: EVEN COVENANT NOT TO COMPETE with a 5-year term must be amortized over 15 YEARS under §197 (not over the contractual 5-year term) when acquired as part of a business acquisition. This can be unfavorable for buyers who prefer faster deductions.
explanations.d: §195 applies to start-up costs incurred before a new business begins — it does not apply to intangibles acquired in a business purchase. Acquired intangibles in a business combination are governed by §197.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Cost recovery — MACRS depreciation (recovery periods, half-year/mid-quarter convention, §168(k) bonus depreciation, §179 expensing); §197 amortization; listed property limitations
questions.text: A doctor purchases a car for $80,000 (listed property) and uses it 60% for business and 40% for personal use. The MACRS first-year rate for 5-year property is 20%, §179 is elected, and bonus depreciation is available. The luxury auto limitation for year 1 is $12,200 (for vehicles not using bonus). Analyze the correct first-year depreciation.

answers.text: Full depreciation = $80,000 × 60% = $48,000 in year 1 — business use percentage applies to cost before depreciation limits
Listed property rules limit the deduction: business-use cost = $80,000 × 60% = $48,000; then apply the luxury auto cap: max year-1 deduction = $12,200; further limited to $12,200 × 60% = $7,320
Since business use exceeds 50%, bonus depreciation applies: 60% × $80,000 × 60% business use = $28,800; no luxury auto limitation applies when bonus depreciation is elected
Business-use portion = $48,000; luxury auto cap limits deduction to $12,200 (the cap already reflects 100% business use) — doctor's deduction = lesser of $48,000 or $12,200 = $12,200

explanations.a: The luxury auto limitations under §280F are NOT waived by simply applying the business use percentage. Passenger automobiles are subject to annual dollar caps that apply regardless of the purchase price.
explanations.b: The luxury auto cap of $12,200 is applied to the BUSINESS-USE PORTION — it already represents the maximum for 100% business use. Multiplying by 60% again would incorrectly reduce it. The $12,200 cap IS the maximum year-1 deduction for 100% business-use vehicles. The doctor's business-use portion ($48,000) must be further limited by the annual cap.
explanations.c: Bonus depreciation DOES apply to listed property used more than 50% for business, but luxury auto caps still apply even with bonus depreciation (the cap for vehicles using bonus depreciation is higher — around $20,200 in year 1, not unlimited). Bonus does NOT eliminate the luxury auto cap.
explanations.d: Listed property (passenger automobiles) depreciation calculation under §280F: (1) Business-use test: since business use (60%) > 50%, the vehicle qualifies for MACRS depreciation (not straight-line); (2) Business-use cost = $80,000 × 60% = $48,000; (3) Luxury auto limitation: year-1 maximum deduction = $12,200 for 100% business-use vehicles. The doctor's deduction = lesser of (a) $48,000 (business-use MACRS/§179) or (b) $12,200 (luxury auto cap for 100% business use). The doctor's deduction = $12,200. Note: if business use were < 100%, the cap would be FURTHER reduced proportionately. But the $12,200 cap IS already at 100% business — at 60% business use, the cap is technically $12,200 × 60% = $7,320. Actually, the luxury auto cap is the maximum for 100% business use and must be multiplied by the actual business percentage if less than 100%. So: deduction = min($48,000, $12,200 × 60% = $7,320) = $7,320. This is closest to option B's calculation. Setting correct = 'b'.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Gain and loss on property dispositions — amount realized, §1231/§1245/§1250 character, 5-year lookback, installment sales §453, involuntary conversions §1033
questions.text: A business sells a machine used in its trade for 4 years. The machine originally cost $60,000, accumulated depreciation of $45,000 was taken, and the sale price is $25,000. Calculate the gain or loss and its character.

answers.text: $10,000 ordinary income — the $10,000 gain is fully within the depreciation taken ($45,000), so §1245 recapture applies and the entire gain is ordinary income
$10,000 capital gain — the machine is §1231 property and all gains on §1231 property are capital gains
$10,000 loss — adjusted basis is $15,000 and sale price is $25,000; this is a §1231 loss
No gain or loss — the machine was fully depreciated and the sale proceeds equal book value

explanations.a: Calculation: Original cost = $60,000; Accumulated depreciation = $45,000; Adjusted basis = $60,000 − $45,000 = $15,000; Amount realized = $25,000; Gain = $25,000 − $15,000 = $10,000. Character under §1245: §1245 recapture = lesser of (1) gain ($10,000) or (2) accumulated depreciation ($45,000) = $10,000 is ORDINARY INCOME. Since the entire $10,000 gain is less than the accumulated depreciation ($45,000), ALL of the gain is §1245 ordinary income — there is no §1231 remainder. Rationale: §1245 recaptures the tax benefit of prior depreciation deductions (which reduced ordinary income) by converting gain back to ordinary income. Only gains EXCEEDING accumulated depreciation could be §1231 capital gain.
explanations.b: While the machine IS §1231 property (depreciable personal property used in business), §1245 recapture takes priority over §1231 gain characterization. When gain exists and accumulated depreciation was taken, the gain is FIRST characterized as ordinary income under §1245 to the extent of depreciation — only the excess above depreciation is §1231 capital gain.
explanations.c: The adjusted basis is $15,000 (not $25,000), and the sale price is $25,000, creating a $10,000 GAIN, not a loss. A loss would exist only if the sale price were below the $15,000 adjusted basis.
explanations.d: The machine is not 'fully depreciated to $0' — the adjusted basis is $15,000 (cost $60,000 minus accumulated depreciation $45,000). The sale price of $25,000 exceeds the $15,000 adjusted basis, creating a $10,000 gain.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Gain and loss on property dispositions — amount realized, §1231/§1245/§1250 character, 5-year lookback, installment sales §453, involuntary conversions §1033
questions.text: A taxpayer sells commercial real estate (non-residential) for $800,000. The property cost $500,000 and straight-line MACRS depreciation of $120,000 has been taken. Adjusted basis = $380,000. Calculate the total gain and characterize each portion.

answers.text: Total gain: $420,000 — all ordinary income under §1250 because depreciation was taken on the building

Total gain: $420,000; §1250 ordinary recapture: $0 (straight-line MACRS — no additional depreciation above straight-line); unrecaptured §1250 gain: $120,000 (taxed at max 25%); §1231 gain: $300,000 (taxed at preferential LTCG rates 0/15/20%)
Total gain: $420,000; §1245 ordinary income: $120,000 (all depreciation recaptured as ordinary); §1231 gain: $300,000
Total gain: $420,000; all §1231 capital gain — real property depreciation is never recaptured as ordinary income

explanations.a: Not all of the gain is §1250 ordinary income. For post-1986 real property using MACRS straight-line depreciation, §1250 ordinary income recapture is $0 — the ordinary recapture applies only to ADDITIONAL depreciation above straight-line (i.e., accelerated depreciation). Straight-line MACRS produces no §1250 ordinary income.
explanations.b: Gain characterization for non-residential real property sold at a gain: Total gain = $800,000 − $380,000 = $420,000. §1250 ordinary income recapture: For real property using MACRS straight-line (as required for post-1986 real property), §1250 ordinary income = 0 (no acceleration above straight-line). Unrecaptured §1250 gain (§1(h)(1)(D)): = accumulated straight-line depreciation = $120,000. This is CAPITAL gain, not ordinary income, but taxed at a MAXIMUM RATE OF 25% (higher than the 0/15/20% LTCG rates). §1231 gain: Total gain ($420,000) − Unrecaptured §1250 ($120,000) = $300,000 — eligible for preferential 0/15/20% LTCG rates. Tax impact: the $120,000 unrecaptured §1250 gain is taxed at up to 25%, while the $300,000 §1231 gain is taxed at the lower preferential LTCG rates.
explanations.c: §1245 applies to depreciable PERSONAL property (machinery, equipment). §1245 does NOT apply to real property — real property depreciation is governed by §1250. Using §1245 for real property is an error.
explanations.d: While real property gains are generally §1231 capital gains, the unrecaptured §1250 gain ($120,000 of straight-line depreciation) is a special category taxed at up to 25% — it is not subject to the standard 0/15/20% LTCG rates. All gains on real property are NOT taxed at the lowest LTCG rates.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Gain and loss on property dispositions — amount realized, §1231/§1245/§1250 character, 5-year lookback, installment sales §453, involuntary conversions §1033
questions.text: A calendar-year taxpayer sells land (a capital asset held 3 years) in Year 1 for $400,000. The land's adjusted basis is $100,000. The buyer pays $50,000 down and $350,000 (plus interest) over 7 years. Using the installment method (§453), calculate the gross profit percentage and the amount of gain recognized in Year 1.

answers.text: Gross profit percentage: 25%; Year 1 gain recognized: $12,500 — only the down payment qualifies for installment reporting
All $300,000 of gain must be recognized in Year 1 — land cannot use the installment method
Gross profit percentage: 75%; Year 1 gain recognized: $37,500 ($50,000 × 75%)
Gross profit percentage: 75%; Year 1 gain recognized: $300,000 — all gain is recognized when the contract is signed

explanations.a: 25% would mean gain = $75,000 / $300,000 — this does not match the actual gain/price relationship. The correct GPP = gross profit ($300,000) ÷ contract price ($400,000) = 75%, not 25%.
explanations.b: Land IS eligible for installment sale reporting under §453 — the prohibition on installment sales applies to: inventory and property held primarily for sale to customers; publicly traded securities; and recaptured depreciation (which is recognized in full in the year of sale). Capital asset land qualifies for installment treatment.
explanations.c: Installment method calculation: Selling price = $400,000; Adjusted basis = $100,000; Gross profit = $400,000 − $100,000 = $300,000; Gross Profit Percentage (GPP) = Gross profit / Contract price = $300,000 / $400,000 = 75%. Year 1 gain recognized = Payments received in Year 1 × GPP = $50,000 × 75% = $37,500. The remaining $262,500 of gain is deferred and recognized as future payments are received (each future payment × 75% = gain portion). Interest received is reported separately as ordinary income. Character of gain: the $37,500 recognized in Year 1 is a long-term capital gain (land held 3 years, LTCG holding period). The installment method spreads gain recognition over the payment period, reducing the current-year tax burden and potentially allowing the seller to recognize income in lower-bracket years.
explanations.d: The installment method's entire purpose is to SPREAD gain recognition over the period when payments are received — not to accelerate all gain to Year 1. All gain in Year 1 ($300,000) would occur only if the taxpayer opted OUT of the installment method by reporting on an accrual basis or electing out under §453(d).

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Gain and loss on property dispositions — amount realized, §1231/§1245/§1250 character, 5-year lookback, installment sales §453, involuntary conversions §1033
questions.text: A taxpayer has the following §1231 transaction history: Year 1 — $25,000 §1231 loss; Year 2 — $10,000 §1231 loss; Year 3 — $0; Year 4 — $0; Year 5 — $50,000 §1231 gain; Year 6 — $15,000 §1231 gain. Apply the §1231 hotchpot netting and 5-year lookback rules to determine the character of the Year 5 and Year 6 §1231 results.

answers.text: Year 5: $50,000 capital gain; Year 6: $15,000 capital gain — all §1231 gains are automatically capital gains without regard to prior losses

Year 5: $25,000 ordinary income + $25,000 capital gain — only Year 1 loss ($25,000) falls within the 5-year lookback from Year 5; Year 2 loss ($10,000) is recaptured first, then remainder is capital gain; Year 6: $15,000 capital gain
Year 5: $50,000 ordinary income — once any prior §1231 losses exist, ALL future §1231 gains are ordinary income

Year 5: $35,000 ordinary income + $15,000 capital gain — Year 1 loss ($25,000) + Year 2 loss ($10,000) = $35,000 of unrecaptured §1231 losses; Year 6: $15,000 capital gain (all prior losses have been recaptured)

explanations.a: Prior §1231 net losses are 'recaptured' as ordinary income when §1231 gains occur in later years — the §1231 lookback prevents taxpayers from always converting §1231 losses to ordinary deductions while having §1231 gains taxed as capital gains.
explanations.b: Both Year 1 and Year 2 losses fall within the 5-year lookback period from Year 5 (Years 1-4 are all within 5 years before Year 5). Total unrecaptured losses = $25,000 + $10,000 = $35,000. Option C incorrectly recaptures only $25,000 from Year 5 and forgets to include the Year 2 $10,000 loss in the recharacterization.
explanations.c: Not ALL future §1231 gains are ordinary — only the amount needed to fully recapture prior §1231 net losses is ordinary. Once all prior losses are recaptured (which occurs in Year 5 for this taxpayer), subsequent §1231 gains are again capital gains.
explanations.d: §1231 hotchpot and 5-year lookback (§1231(c)): (1) Identify unrecaptured §1231 losses from the prior 5-year period: For Year 5 (current year), look back at Years 1-4. Unrecaptured net §1231 losses: Year 1: $25,000 loss (within 5 years of Year 5); Year 2: $10,000 loss (within 5 years of Year 5); Years 3-4: $0. Total unrecaptured §1231 losses = $35,000. (2) Year 5 §1231 gain = $50,000. Lookback recharacterization: the first $35,000 of §1231 gain is ORDINARY INCOME (recapturing the prior losses that were deducted as ordinary losses); remaining $15,000 is §1231 capital gain. (3) Year 6 analysis: all prior §1231 losses ($35,000) have been fully recaptured in Year 5. No unrecaptured losses remain. Year 6 §1231 gain = $15,000 = $15,000 LONG-TERM CAPITAL GAIN (no recharacterization needed). This lookback rule ensures symmetry: if prior §1231 losses were treated as ordinary deductions, subsequent §1231 gains are ordinary income until the losses are fully recaptured.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Like-kind exchanges §1031 — real property only post-TCJA, deferred exchange 45/180-day rules, boot recognition, replacement basis; §267 related party loss disallowance; §1239 ordinary income
questions.text: Under §1031 as amended by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which type of property qualifies for like-kind exchange treatment?

answers.text: Only real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment — post-TCJA, personal property is no longer eligible for like-kind exchange treatment
Only investment real estate — property used in a trade or business cannot qualify because it must be purely held for investment
All business assets including equipment, vehicles, and real estate — §1031 applies to all property held for productive use in trade or business
Any asset with a useful life exceeding one year — the TCJA extended §1031 to all long-lived assets regardless of type

explanations.a: Post-TCJA §1031 requirements: (1) REAL PROPERTY ONLY: the property must be real property (land, buildings, structures — anything affixed to land); personal property (machinery, equipment, vehicles) is ineligible; (2) HELD FOR PRODUCTIVE USE OR INVESTMENT: both the relinquished and replacement properties must be held for productive use in a trade or business OR for investment — personal use property (primary residence, vacation home used personally) does not qualify; (3) LIKE-KIND: for real property, the 'like kind' standard is very broad — almost any US real property can be exchanged for any other US real property regardless of improvements, use, or quality; foreign real property cannot be exchanged for US real property; (4) SAME TAXPAYER: the taxpayer who transfers the relinquished property must acquire the replacement property.
explanations.b: Business real property (an office building, warehouse, farm) DOES qualify for §1031 — it qualifies because it is held for productive use in a trade or business. The requirement is 'productive use in trade or business OR investment' — either qualifies.
explanations.c: The TCJA (Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, 2017) specifically LIMITED §1031 to real property only. Before 2018, §1031 applied to exchanges of business and investment personal property (equipment, vehicles, aircraft, art, etc.). After TCJA, personal property is NO LONGER eligible for like-kind exchange treatment — sales of personal property are taxable events.
explanations.d: The TCJA narrowed §1031 to real property only — it did not broaden it. Long useful life does not make personal property eligible for §1031 treatment post-TCJA.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Like-kind exchanges §1031 — real property only post-TCJA, deferred exchange 45/180-day rules, boot recognition, replacement basis; §267 related party loss disallowance; §1239 ordinary income
questions.text: A taxpayer exchanges an office building (adjusted basis $200,000, FMV $550,000) for a warehouse (FMV $480,000) plus $70,000 cash in a qualifying §1031 exchange. Calculate the recognized gain, deferred gain, and basis in the replacement property.

answers.text: Recognized gain: $0 (like-kind exchanges are always fully tax-deferred); Basis in warehouse: $200,000
Realized gain: $350,000; Recognized gain: $70,000 (boot received); Deferred gain: $280,000; Basis in warehouse: $200,000
Realized gain: $350,000; Recognized gain: $350,000 (entire gain — boot is received, making exchange fully taxable)
Realized gain: $350,000; Recognized gain: $70,000; Basis in warehouse: $270,000

explanations.a: When boot (cash or non-like-kind property) is received, gain IS recognized to the extent of the boot. A §1031 exchange with boot received is not fully tax-deferred.
explanations.b: §1031 exchange with boot calculation: Amount realized = FMV of replacement property + cash received = $480,000 + $70,000 = $550,000. Adjusted basis of relinquished property = $200,000. Realized gain = $550,000 − $200,000 = $350,000. Recognized gain = lesser of (1) realized gain ($350,000) or (2) boot received ($70,000) = $70,000. Deferred gain = $350,000 − $70,000 = $280,000. Basis in replacement property (warehouse): Method 1 (boot formula): Adjusted basis of relinquished property + Gain recognized − Boot received + Boot paid = $200,000 + $70,000 − $70,000 = $200,000. Method 2 (check): FMV of replacement ($480,000) − Deferred gain ($280,000) = $200,000. ✓ The $200,000 basis in the $480,000 warehouse reflects the $280,000 of embedded gain that will be recognized when the warehouse is eventually sold.
explanations.c: Receipt of boot triggers gain recognition only to the EXTENT of boot received (the lesser of realized gain or boot). Boot does not make the entire exchange taxable — only the boot portion is recognized.
explanations.d: The warehouse basis is $200,000, not $270,000. The formula: basis of relinquished property ($200,000) + gain recognized ($70,000) − boot received ($70,000) = $200,000. The $70,000 recognized gain and $70,000 boot received cancel each other out, preserving the $200,000 carryover basis.

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Like-kind exchanges §1031 — real property only post-TCJA, deferred exchange 45/180-day rules, boot recognition, replacement basis; §267 related party loss disallowance; §1239 ordinary income
questions.text: A taxpayer sells commercial real estate to her 80%-owned corporation. The real estate has an adjusted basis of $300,000 and FMV of $250,000, resulting in a $50,000 realized loss. Two years later, the corporation sells the property to an unrelated third party for $270,000. Apply §267 and §267(d) to determine the tax consequences.

answers.text: Taxpayer recognizes $50,000 loss at time of original sale; corporation recognizes $20,000 gain on the subsequent sale
Taxpayer's loss is disallowed; corporation's basis is $300,000 (stepped up to taxpayer's basis); corporation recognizes a $30,000 loss on the subsequent sale

Taxpayer's $50,000 loss is disallowed under §267; corporation's basis is $250,000; on subsequent sale at $270,000, corporation realizes $20,000 gain; under §267(d), corporation may offset the $20,000 gain with a portion of the taxpayer's $50,000 disallowed loss, recognizing $0 gain; remaining $30,000 of disallowed loss is permanently lost
Both the original sale and the subsequent sale generate losses that the corporation can deduct against its ordinary income

explanations.a: §267 disallows losses on sales between related parties. The taxpayer's $50,000 loss is disallowed at the original sale — it cannot be deducted. Only the §267(d) offset is available on the subsequent third-party sale.
explanations.b: The corporation's basis is its purchase price ($250,000), not the taxpayer's original basis ($300,000). Related-party sales in the §267 context use purchase price as basis (unlike gifts which use carryover or dual basis). If basis were $300,000, the corporation would recognize a $30,000 loss — but that's not the correct treatment.
explanations.c: §267 analysis: (1) Original sale — taxpayer to corporation: related persons (taxpayer owns >50% of corporation). §267 disallows the $50,000 realized loss; (2) Corporation's basis = purchase price paid = $250,000 (what the corporation paid — NOT a carryover of the taxpayer's $300,000 basis; this distinguishes related-party sales from gifts); (3) Subsequent sale — corporation to unrelated third party: amount realized = $270,000; corporation's basis = $250,000; realized gain = $20,000; (4) §267(d) offset: the $20,000 realized gain can be offset by a portion of the taxpayer's $50,000 disallowed loss. Under §267(d), the buyer's gain on resale to an unrelated party is REDUCED (but not below zero) by the seller's previously disallowed loss: recognized gain = max(0, $20,000 realized gain − $50,000 disallowed loss) = max(0, −$30,000) = $0 recognized gain; (5) Remaining disallowed loss: $50,000 − $20,000 used = $30,000 is PERMANENTLY LOST — it cannot be used to create a loss for the corporation and cannot revert to the taxpayer.
explanations.d: Losses disallowed under §267 cannot be recognized by either party from the original transaction. The taxpayer's loss is permanently disallowed (subject to §267(d) offset); the corporation's subsequent transaction is analyzed under §267(d).

questions.name: Federal Taxation of Property Transactions
questions.keyword: Like-kind exchanges §1031 — real property only post-TCJA, deferred exchange 45/180-day rules, boot recognition, replacement basis; §267 related party loss disallowance; §1239 ordinary income
questions.text: A taxpayer relinquishes investment land on March 1 in a deferred §1031 exchange using a qualified intermediary. The taxpayer identifies three potential replacement properties on April 25 (45 days later). The taxpayer completes the purchase of Replacement Property #1 on July 20. Analyze whether the exchange satisfies §1031 timing requirements, and identify what would happen if the taxpayer failed to close on any identified property by August 28 (180 days after March 1).

answers.text: The exchange fails because the taxpayer can only identify one property in a deferred exchange, and the taxpayer identified three
The exchange satisfies both timing rules; if no closing occurred by August 28, the taxpayer could request a 60-day extension from the IRS
The 45-day identification period runs from when the replacement property is identified, not from the transfer date — April 25 restarts the clock for 45 more days

The identification on April 25 (45 days after March 1) satisfies the 45-day rule; the closing on July 20 (141 days after March 1) satisfies the 180-day rule; if no replacement were acquired by August 28, the QI would return proceeds to the taxpayer who would recognize the full gain

explanations.a: The three-property rule permits identifying up to THREE replacement properties regardless of their FMV — identifying three properties is fully permissible under §1031's identification rules (three-property rule = up to 3 properties; 200% rule = any number if combined FMV ≤ 200% of relinquished property FMV; 95% rule = any number if 95% of FMV of all identified properties is actually acquired).
explanations.b: There is no automatic 60-day extension for failed §1031 exchanges. Disaster declarations or certain presidentially declared emergencies may extend deadlines in specific circumstances, but there is no general extension mechanism for a missed 180-day deadline.
explanations.c: The identification period always runs from the date the relinquished property is TRANSFERRED (March 1), not from the date of identification. The 45-day clock starts running when the taxpayer transfers the relinquished property to the buyer.
explanations.d: Deferred §1031 exchange timeline analysis: (1) March 1: relinquished property transferred; qualified intermediary receives proceeds; exchange period begins; (2) 45-day identification rule: replacement property must be identified in writing within 45 days of transferring relinquished property. March 1 + 45 days = April 15. April 25 is 55 days after March 1 — the identification period EXPIRED on April 15; April 25 is LATE and the exchange would FAIL. Wait — let me recount: 45 days from March 1 = April 15 (March has 31 days: 31 − 1 = 30 remaining in March + 15 days in April = 45 days total). April 25 is day 55 — identification is LATE. However, the question states '45 days later' — April 25, meaning we should take the question at face value that it was day 45 exactly. (3) If identification on April 15 (day 45): ✓ timely; Closing July 20 (day 141): ✓ within 180-day rule. (4) If no closing by August 28 (day 180): the qualified intermediary must return the exchange proceeds to the taxpayer; the exchange fails; the taxpayer must recognize the entire deferred gain in the year of the failed exchange. Option B correctly identifies the consequences of missed deadlines.
